paragraphs.heading: The biggest black holes
paragraphs.text: A supermassive black hole is the largest kind of black hole. A black hole is a region of space left behind by gravitational collapse, and nothing can get out of it, not even light. The supermassive ones are usually defined as having more than 100,000 times the mass of the Sun. Some weigh several billion Suns.

paragraphs.heading: One in nearly every big galaxy
paragraphs.text: Evidence suggests almost every large galaxy has one at its centre. Our own Milky Way does, and it matches a radio source called Sagittarius A*. When gas from between the stars falls onto one of these giants, a process called accretion, it powers active galactic nuclei and quasars. The Event Horizon Telescope has directly imaged two of them: Sagittarius A* and the one at the heart of Messier 87, a giant elliptical galaxy.

paragraphs.heading: A surprisingly gentle edge
paragraphs.text: Near the event horizon, the tidal force is much weaker for a supermassive black hole. It shrinks with the square of the mass. Someone standing at the event horizon of a 10-million-solar-mass black hole would feel about the same head-to-foot stretch as someone standing on Earth. Unlike with stellar-mass black holes, the strong stretching would only begin very deep inside the horizon.

paragraphs.heading: Less dense than water
paragraphs.text: Oddly, a supermassive black hole can have a lower average density than water. Here density means its mass divided by the volume inside its Schwarzschild radius, the radius of its event horizon. That radius grows in step with the mass, while the volume grows with the cube of the radius. So density goes down as one over the mass squared, and bigger black holes are less dense on average. For one of about a billion solar masses, the horizon radius is about 19 AU, comparable to the size of Uranus's orbit.

paragraphs.heading: The very largest
paragraphs.text: Some astronomers call black holes above 5 billion solar masses ultramassive, although the term is not widely used. Candidates include the central black holes of NGC 4889, NGC 6166, TON 618 and ESO 444-46. Some studies suggest that a black hole feeding from a disc of gas usually tops out at around 50 billion solar masses. A 2020 study proposed that even bigger stupendously large black holes, above 100 billion solar masses, could exist, perhaps including the one in Phoenix A.

paragraphs.heading: How the idea arose
paragraphs.text: The trail starts in 1963, when Maarten Schmidt studied the radio source 3C 273. Its light turned out to be hydrogen lines shifted toward the red, and Hubble's law put it several billion light-years away, so it had to be giving off the energy of hundreds of galaxies. Its light changed so quickly that the glowing region was likely a parsec or less across. In 1964 Salpeter and Yakov Zeldovich proposed that matter falling onto a massive compact object, of about 10⁸ solar masses, could explain quasars. In 1969 Donald Lynden-Bell added that the falling gas would form a flat disc spiralling inward.

paragraphs.heading: Finding ours
paragraphs.text: In 1971 Donald Lynden-Bell and Martin Rees suggested that the centre of the Milky Way would hold a massive black hole. In February 1974, Bruce Balick and Robert Brown found and named Sagittarius A* with the Green Bank Interferometer. The radio source they found was dense and held still by its own gravity. It was the first sign that a supermassive black hole lies at the centre of our galaxy.
